cues.en: Take one plus two plus four plus eight, and continue on and on adding the next power of two up to infinity.
cues.zh: 取 1 加 2 加 4 加 8，然后不断加上下一个 2 的幂，一直到无穷。

cues.en: This might seem crazy, but there's a sense in which this infinite sum equals negative one.
cues.zh: 这看起来可能很疯狂，但某种意义上，这个无穷和等于负一。

cues.en: If you're like me, this feels strange or obviously false when you first see it. But I promise you, by the end of this video, you and I will make it make sense.
cues.zh: 如果你像我一样，第一次看到它时会觉得奇怪，或者显然不对。但我保证，到这个视频结束时，你我会把它讲明白。

cues.en: To do this, we need to back up, and you and I will walk through what it might feel like to discover convergent infinite sums, those ones that at least seem to make sense, to define what they really mean, then to discover this crazy equation and stumble upon new forms of math where it makes sense.
cues.zh: 为了做到这一点，我们需要退一步。你我会一起体会：发现收敛的无穷和——那些至少看起来说得通的无穷和——是什么感觉；定义它们到底意味着什么；然后再发现这个疯狂的等式，并偶然踏入让它在其中说得通的新数学形式。

cues.en: Imagine that you are an early mathematician in the process of discovering that one half plus one fourth plus one eighth plus one sixteenth on and on up to infinity, whatever that means, equals one. And imagine that you needed to define what it means to add infinitely many things for your friends to take you seriously.
cues.zh: 想象你是一位早期数学家，正在发现 1/2 + 1/4 + 1/8 + 1/16 一直加到无穷——不管那是什么意思——等于 1。再想象你需要定义“把无穷多个东西加起来”是什么意思，才能让朋友们认真对待你。

cues.en: What would that feel like? Frankly, I have no idea, and I imagine that more than anything, it feels like being wrong or stuck most of the time. But I'll give my best guess at one way that the successful parts of it might go.
cues.zh: 那会是什么感觉？坦白说，我完全不知道；我想，大多数时候更像是觉得自己错了或卡住了。但我会尽力猜一种可能：其中成功的部分会怎样展开。

cues.en: One day, you're pondering the nature of distances between objects,
cues.zh: 有一天，你在思考物体之间距离的本质，

cues.en: and how no matter how close two things are, it seems that they can always be brought a little bit closer together without touching.
cues.zh: 以及无论两个东西多近，似乎总能不接触地把它们再拉近一点。

cues.en: Fond of math as you are, you wanna capture this paradoxical feeling with numbers.
cues.zh: 你热爱数学，于是想用数字捕捉这种悖论般的感觉。

cues.en: So you imagine placing the two objects on the number line, the first at zero, the second at one.
cues.zh: 于是你想象把两个物体放在数轴上，第一个在 0，第二个在 1。

cues.en: Then you march the first object towards the second, such that with each step, the distance between them is cut in half.
cues.zh: 然后你让第一个物体朝第二个移动，每一步都把两者之间的距离减半。

cues.en: You keep track of the numbers this object touches during its march, writing down one half, one half plus a fourth, one half plus a fourth plus an eighth, and so on.
cues.zh: 你记录这个物体行进途中经过的数字：写下 1/2、1/2 + 1/4、1/2 + 1/4 + 1/8，依此类推。

cues.en: That is, each number is naturally written as a slightly longer sum with one more power of two in it.
cues.zh: 也就是说，每个数自然都写成一个稍长的和，其中多包含一个 2 的幂。

cues.en: As such, you're tempted to say that if these numbers approach anything,
cues.zh: 于是你忍不住想说，如果这些数趋近于某个东西，

cues.en: we should be able to write this thing down as a sum that contains the reciprocal of every power of two.
cues.zh: 我们应该能把这东西写成一个和，包含每个 2 的幂的倒数。

cues.en: On the other hand, we can see geometrically that these numbers approach one. So what you want to say is that one and some kind of infinite sum are the same thing.
cues.zh: 另一方面，从几何上能看出这些数趋近于 1。所以你想说的是，1 和某种无穷和是同一回事。

cues.en: If your education was too formal, you'd write the statement off as ridiculous. Clearly, you can't add infinitely many things. No human, computer, or physical thing ever could perform such a task. If, however, you approach math with a healthy irreverence,
cues.zh: 如果你的教育太形式化，你会把这说法斥为荒唐。显然，你不能把无穷多个东西加起来。没有人、计算机或任何物理实体能完成这种任务。不过，如果你带着一种健康的“不敬”态度接近数学，

cues.en: you'll stand brave in the face of ridiculousness
cues.zh: 你就会勇敢地面对这种荒唐，

cues.en: and try to make sense out of this nonsense that you wrote down, since it kinda feels like nature gave it to you. So how exactly do you, dear mathematician,
cues.zh: 并试着让你写下的这堆胡话变得有意义，因为它多少像是自然塞给你的。那么，亲爱的数学家，你究竟要怎样

cues.en: go about defining infinite sums?
cues.zh: 定义无穷和呢？

cues.en: Well practiced in math that you are, you know that finding the right definitions is less about generating new thoughts than it is about dissecting old thoughts. So you go back to how you came across this fuzzy discovery.
cues.zh: 你数学已经很熟练，所以知道：找到正确的定义，与其说是产生新想法，不如说是剖析旧想法。于是你回到自己最初是如何遇上这个模糊发现的。

cues.en: At no point did you actually perform infinitely many operations.
cues.zh: 你其实从未真正进行过无限多次运算。

cues.en: You had a list of numbers, a list that could keep going forever if you had the time,
cues.zh: 你有一个数字列表，只要你有时间，这个列表可以一直延续下去，

cues.en: and each number came from a perfectly reasonable finite sum.
cues.zh: 而且每个数都来自一个完全合理的有限和。

cues.en: You noticed that the numbers in this list approach one, But what do you mean by approach?
cues.zh: 你注意到这个列表中的数趋近于 1。但“趋近”是什么意思？

cues.en: It's not just that the distance between each number and one gets smaller, because for that matter, the distance between each number and two also gets smaller.
cues.zh: 并不只是每个数到 1 的距离在变小，因为照这么说，每个数到 2 的距离也在变小。

cues.en: After thinking about it, you realize what makes one special is that your numbers can get arbitrarily
cues.zh: 想了想，你意识到 1 之所以特别，是因为你的数可以任意地

cues.en: close to one, which is to say, no matter how small your desired distance, one one hundredth, one one millionth, or one over the largest number you could write down, if you go down your list long enough, the numbers will eventually fall within that tiny tiny distance of one.
cues.zh: 接近 1。也就是说，无论你期望的距离多小——百分之一、百万分之一，还是你能写下的最大数分之一——只要沿着列表走得足够远，这些数最终都会落入离 1 那一点点极小的距离内。

cues.en: Retrospectively,
cues.zh: 事后看来，

cues.en: this might seem like the clear way to solidify what you mean by approach,
cues.zh: 这似乎是明确“趋近”含义的清晰办法，

cues.en: but as a first time endeavor, it's actually incredibly clever.
cues.zh: 但作为第一次尝试，这其实非常聪明。

cues.en: Now you pull out your pin and scribble down the definition for what it means for an infinite sum to equal some number, say x.
cues.zh: 现在你拿出笔，草草写下“无穷和等于某个数（比如 x）”的定义。

cues.en: It means that when you generate a list of numbers by cutting off your sum at finite points,
cues.zh: 意思是，当你在有限点截断求和、生成一个数列时，

cues.en: the numbers in this list approach x in the sense that no matter how small the distance you choose, at some point down the list, all the numbers start falling within that distance of x.
cues.zh: 这个数列中的数会趋近于 x；也就是说，无论你选择的距离多小，沿着数列走到某一点后，所有数都会开始落入离 x 不超过该距离的范围内。

cues.en: In doing this, you just invented some math,
cues.zh: 这样做，你刚刚发明了一些数学，

cues.en: but it never felt like you were pulling things out of thin air. You were just trying to justify what it was that the universe gave you in the first place.
cues.zh: 但感觉并不像是凭空捏造。你只是在努力说明，宇宙最初给你的东西究竟是什么。

cues.en: You might wonder if you can find other, more general truths about these infinite sums that you just invented.
cues.zh: 你可能想知道，对于你刚发明的这些无穷和，能不能找到其他更一般的真理。

cues.en: To do so, you look for where you made any arbitrary decisions.
cues.zh: 为此，你要找出自己在哪里做了任意选择。

cues.en: For instance, when you were shrinking the distance between your objects, cutting the interval into pieces of size one half, one fourth, etcetera,
cues.zh: 例如，当你缩小物体之间的距离，把区间切成大小为二分之一、四分之一等的小段时，

cues.en: you could have chosen a proportion other than one half. You could have instead cut your interval into pieces of size nine tenths and one tenth, and then cut that rightmost piece into the same proportions,
cues.zh: 你本可以选择二分之一以外的比例。你也可以把区间切成十分之九和十分之一两段，然后按同样比例切最右边那段，

cues.en: giving you smaller pieces of size nine one hundredths and one one hundredth. Then cut that tiny piece of size one one hundredth similarly.
cues.zh: 得到大小为百分之九和百分之一的小段。再把大小为百分之一的那一小段同样切分。

cues.en: Continuing on and on, you'd see that nine tenths plus nine one hundredths plus nine one thousandths on and on up to infinity equals one.
cues.zh: 一直继续下去，你会看到十分之九加百分之九加千分之九，如此一直到无穷，等于一。

cues.en: A fact more popularly written as point nine repeating equals one.
cues.zh: 一个更广为人知的写法是：0.999… 等于 1。

cues.en: To all of your friends who insist that this doesn't equal one and it just approaches it, you can now just smile because you know that with infinite sums, to approach and to equal mean the same thing.
cues.zh: 至于那些坚持认为它不等于 1、只是无限接近 1 的朋友们，你现在可以微微一笑，因为你知道了：在无穷级数里，“接近”和“等于”是同一个意思。

cues.en: To be general about it, let's say that you cut your interval into pieces of size p and one minus p,
cues.zh: 更一般地说，假设你把区间切成大小为 p 和 1 减 p 的两段，

cues.en: where p represents any number between zero and one.
cues.zh: 其中 p 代表 0 到 1 之间的任意数。

cues.en: Cutting the piece of size p in similar proportions, we now get pieces of size p times one minus p and p squared.
cues.zh: 再按相同比例切分大小为 p 的那一段，我们就得到大小为 p 乘 1 减 p 和 p 平方的两段。

cues.en: Continuing in this fashion, always cutting up the rightmost piece into those same proportions,
cues.zh: 照这样继续下去，总是把最右边那段按同样的比例切开，

cues.en: you'll find that one minus p, plus p times one minus p, plus p squared times one minus p, on and on, always adding p to the next power times one minus p, equals one.
cues.zh: 你会发现：1 减 p，加上 p 乘 1 减 p，加上 p 平方乘 1 减 p，一直下去，总是加上 p 的下一个幂乘 1 减 p，结果等于 1。

cues.en: Dividing both sides by one minus p, we get this nice formula.
cues.zh: 两边同除以 1 减 p，就得到了这个漂亮的公式。

cues.en: In this formula, the universe is offered a weird form of nonsense.
cues.zh: 在这个公式里，宇宙向你抛出了一种奇怪的荒谬形式。

cues.en: Even though the way that you discovered it only makes sense for values of p between zero and one, the right hand side still makes sense when you replace p with any other number, except maybe for one.
cues.zh: 尽管你发现它的方式只对 0 到 1 之间的 p 值有意义，但当你把 p 替换成其他任何数时，右边仍然说得通，除了 p 等于 1 可能是个例外。

cues.en: For instance, plugging in negative one, the equation reads one minus one plus one minus one on and on forever alternating between the two equals one half,
cues.zh: 比如代入负 1，这个等式读作：1 减 1 加 1 减 1，永远交替下去，等于二分之一，

cues.en: which feels both pretty silly and kinda like the only thing that it could be.
cues.zh: 这既感觉相当傻，又有点像是它唯一可能的取值。

cues.en: Plugging in two, the equation reads one plus two plus four plus eight on and on to infinity
cues.zh: 代入 2，这个等式读作：1 加 2 加 4 加 8，一直加到无穷，

cues.en: equals negative one, something which doesn't even seem reasonable.
cues.zh: 等于负 1，这看起来就完全不合理了。

cues.en: On the one hand, rigor would dictate that you ignore these since the definition of infinite sums doesn't apply in these cases. The list of numbers that you generate by cutting off the sum at finite points doesn't approach anything.
cues.zh: 一方面，严谨性会要求你无视这些情况，因为无穷级数的定义在这里并不适用。你在有限项处截断所得的那串数字，并不逼近任何东西。

cues.en: But you're a mathematician, not a robot.
cues.zh: 但你是数学家，不是机器人。

cues.en: So you don't let the fact that something is nonsensical stop you.
cues.zh: 所以你不会因为某件事荒谬就停下脚步。

cues.en: I will leave this sum for another day so that we can jump directly into this monster.
cues.zh: 这个和我们就改日再谈，好让我们直接跳到这只怪物面前。

cues.en: First, to clean things up, notice what you get when you cut off the sum at finite points.
cues.zh: 首先，为了简化问题，注意一下在有限项处截断这个和会得到什么。

cues.en: One, three,
cues.zh: 一，三，

cues.en: seven,
cues.zh: 七，
十五，
三十一。

cues.en: They're all one less than a power of two.
cues.zh: 它们都比 2 的某个幂小 1。

cues.en: In general, when you add up the first n powers of two, you get two to the n plus one minus one, which this animation hopefully makes clear.
cues.zh: 一般来说，把 2 的前 n 个幂加起来，会得到 2 的 n 加 1 次方减 1，希望这个动画能说清楚这一点。

cues.en: You decide to humor the universe and pretend that these numbers, all one less than a power two, actually do approach negative one. It will prove to be cleaner if we add one to everything and say that the powers of two approach zero.
cues.zh: 你决定迁就一下宇宙，假装这些比 2 的幂小 1 的数真的逼近负 1。如果我们把所有东西都加 1，说成 2 的幂逼近 0，问题会变得更简洁。

cues.en: Is there any way that this can make sense?
cues.zh: 这有没有可能说得通呢？

cues.en: In effect, what you're trying to do is make this formula more general by saying that it applies to all numbers, not just those between zero and one.
cues.zh: 实际上，你想做的是让这个公式更一般化，宣称它适用于所有数，而不仅仅是 0 到 1 之间的数。

cues.en: Again, to make things more general, you look for any place where you made an arbitrary choice.
cues.zh: 再说，为了更一般化，你要找出自己做任意选择的地方。

cues.en: Here, that place turns out to be very sneaky.
cues.zh: 而在这里，这个地方其实非常隐蔽。

cues.en: So sneaky, in fact, that it took mathematicians until the twentieth century to find it.
cues.zh: 隐蔽到数学家直到 20 世纪才找到它。

cues.en: It's the way that we define distance between two rational numbers.
cues.zh: 它就是我们对两个有理数之间距离的定义方式。

cues.en: That is to say, organizing them on a line might not be the only reasonable way to organize them.
cues.zh: 也就是说，把它们排成一条线，可能并不是唯一合理的组织方式。

cues.en: The notion of distance is essentially a function that takes in two numbers and outputs a number indicating how far apart they are.
cues.zh: 距离这个概念本质上是一个函数：输入两个数，输出一个表示它们相隔多远的数。

cues.en: You could come up with a completely random notion of distance where two is seven away from three and one half is four fifths away from a 100 and all sorts of things. But if you want to actually use a new distance function the way that you use the familiar distance function, it should share some of the same properties.
cues.zh: 你完全可以随便发明一种距离概念，比如让 2 离 3 有 7 那么远，让 1/2 离 100 有 4/5 那么远，诸如此类。但如果你真想像使用熟悉的距离函数那样使用新的距离函数，它就应该具备一些相同的性质。

cues.en: For example, the distance between two numbers shouldn't change if you shift them both by the same amount.
cues.zh: 例如，如果两个数同时平移相同的量，它们之间的距离不应该改变。

cues.en: So zero and four should be the same distance away as one and five or two and six, even if that same distance is something other than four as we're used to.
cues.zh: 所以 0 和 4 的距离，应该与 1 和 5、2 和 6 的距离相同，即使这个距离不是我们习惯的 4。

cues.en: Keeping things general, the distance between two numbers shouldn't change if you add the same amount to both of them. Let's call this property shift invariance.
cues.zh: 保持一般性，如果给两个数都加上相同的量，它们之间的距离不应该改变。我们把这个性质叫作平移不变性。

cues.en: There are other properties that you want your notion of distance to have as well, like the triangle inequality.
cues.zh: 你还会希望距离概念具备其他性质，比如三角不等式。

cues.en: But before we start worrying about those, let's start imagining what notion of distance could possibly make powers of two approach zero,
cues.zh: 但在开始担心这些之前，我们先来设想：什么样的距离概念可能让 2 的幂趋近于零，

cues.en: and which is shift invariant.
cues.zh: 并且具有平移不变性。

cues.en: At first, you might toil for a while to find a frame of mind where this doesn't feel like utter nonsense.
cues.zh: 一开始，你可能得琢磨一阵，才能找到一种不觉得这纯属胡扯的视角。

cues.en: But with enough time and a bit of luck, you might think to organize your numbers into rooms, subrooms,
cues.zh: 但如果时间足够，再加上一点运气，你可能会想到把数组织成房间、子房间、

cues.en: sub subrooms, and so on.
cues.zh: 子子房间，等等。

cues.en: You think of zero as being in the same room as all of the powers of two greater than one,
cues.zh: 你把 0 看作和所有大于 1 的 2 的幂在同一个房间里，

cues.en: as being in the same sub room as all powers of two greater than two,
cues.zh: 看作和所有大于 2 的 2 的幂在同一个子房间里，

cues.en: as being in the same sub sub room as powers of two greater than four, and so on, with infinitely many smaller and smaller rooms.
cues.zh: 看作和所有大于 4 的 2 的幂在同一个子子房间里，依此类推，还有无穷多个越来越小的房间。

cues.en: It's pretty hard to draw infinitely many things, so I'm only gonna draw four room sizes, but keep in the back of your mind that this process should be able to go on forever.
cues.zh: 画出无穷多个东西挺难的，所以我只画四种大小的房间，但你要记住，这个过程应该可以永远继续下去。

cues.en: If we think of every number as lying in a hierarchy of rooms, not just zero, shift invariance will tell us where all of the numbers must fall.
cues.zh: 如果我们把每个数都看作处在一种房间层级中，而不只是 0，那么平移不变性会告诉我们所有数必须落在哪里。

cues.en: For instance, one should be as far away from three as two is from zero.
cues.zh: 比如，1 到 3 的距离，应该和 2 到 0 的距离一样。

cues.en: Likewise, the distance between zero and four should be the same as that between one and five, two and six, and three and seven.
cues.zh: 同样，0 和 4 之间的距离，应该等于 1 和 5、2 和 6、3 和 7 之间的距离。

cues.en: Continuing like this, you'll see which rooms, subrooms,
cues.zh: 照这样继续，你就能看出哪些房间、子房间，

cues.en: sub subrooms, and so on successive numbers must fall into.
cues.zh: 子子房间，依此类推，依次该归入哪些数字。

cues.en: You can also deduce where negative numbers must fall. For example, negative one has to be in the same room as one,
cues.zh: 你也可以推断负数该归到哪里。比如，负一必须和一在同一个房间，

cues.en: in the same subroom as three,
cues.zh: 和三在同一个子房间，

cues.en: the same sub subroom as seven,
cues.zh: 和七在同一个子子房间，

cues.en: and so on, always in smaller and smaller rooms with numbers one less than a power of two, because zero is in smaller and smaller rooms with the powers of two.
cues.zh: 以此类推，房间会越来越小，里面的数字总比某个二的幂小一，因为零所在的房间会随着二的幂不断变小。

cues.en: So how do you turn this general idea of closeness based on rooms and subrooms into an actual distance function?
cues.zh: 那么，怎样把这种基于房间和子房间的邻近关系，转化为一个真正的距离函数呢？

cues.en: You can't take this drawing too literally since it makes one look very close to fourteen and zero very far from 13,
cues.zh: 不能把这张图看得太字面，因为它会让人觉得一和十四很近，而零离十三很远，

cues.en: even though shift invariance should imply that they're the same distance away.
cues.zh: 尽管平移不变性意味着它们的距离应该相同。

cues.en: Again, in the actual process of discovery, you might toil away scribbling through many sheets of paper. But if you have the idea that the only thing which should matter in determining the distance between two objects is the size of the smallest room they share,
cues.zh: 再说一次，实际探索时，你可能会埋头在许多张纸上反复演算。但如果你想到，决定两个对象之间距离的唯一因素，应该是它们共同所在的最小房间有多大，

cues.en: you might come up with the following.
cues.zh: 就可能得到下面这个定义。

cues.en: Any numbers lying in different large yellow rooms are distance one from each other.
cues.zh: 落在不同的大黄色房间里的任意两个数，距离都是一。

cues.en: Those which are in the same large room, but not in the same orange sub room are a distance one half from each other.
cues.zh: 在同一个大房间里、但不在同一个橙色子房间里的数，彼此距离是二分之一。

cues.en: Those that are in the same orange subroom but not in the same sub subroom
cues.zh: 在同一个橙色子房间里、但不在同一个子子房间里的数，

cues.en: are a distance one fourth from each other.
cues.zh: 彼此距离是四分之一。

cues.en: And you continue like this, using the reciprocals of larger and larger powers of two to indicate closeness.
cues.zh: 照这样继续下去，用越来越大的二的幂的倒数来表示越来越近。

cues.en: We won't do it in this video, but see if you can reason about which rooms other rational numbers, like one third and one half, should fall into.
cues.zh: 这期视频里不会展开，不过你可以试着推理一下，像三分之一和二分之一这样的其他有理数应该落在哪些房间里。

cues.en: And see if you can prove why this notion of distance satisfies many of the nice properties we expect from a distance function, like the triangle inequality.
cues.zh: 也可以试着证明，这种距离满足距离函数的许多良好性质，比如三角不等式。

cues.en: Here, I'll just say that this notion of distance is a perfectly legitimate one. We call it the two adic metric, and it falls into a general family of distance functions called the p adic metrics, where p stands for any prime number.
cues.zh: 这里我只说，这种距离完全合理。我们称之为二进赋值度量，它属于一类称为 p 进度量的距离函数，p 可以是任意素数。

cues.en: These metrics give rise to a completely new type of number, neither real nor complex, and have become a central notion in modern number theory.
cues.zh: 这些度量会引出一种全新的数，既不是实数也不是复数，并已成为现代数论的核心概念。

cues.en: Using the two addict metric, the fact that the sum of all powers of two equals negative one actually makes sense because the numbers one, three, seven, 15, 31, and so on genuinely approach negative one.
cues.zh: 按照二进赋值度量，所有二的幂之和等于负一这件事其实说得通，因为一、三、七、十五、三十一等数确实越来越接近负一。

cues.en: This parable does not actually portray the historical trajectory of discoveries,
cues.zh: 这个寓言并没有真正呈现相关发现的历史进程，

cues.en: but nevertheless,
cues.zh: 但即便如此，

cues.en: I still think it's a good illustration of a recurring pattern in the discovery of math.
cues.zh: 我仍觉得它很好地说明了数学发现中反复出现的一种模式。

cues.en: First, nature hands you something that's ill defined or even nonsensical.
cues.zh: 首先，大自然会交给你一些定义模糊、甚至毫无意义的东西。

cues.en: Then you define new concepts that make this fuzzy discovery make sense. And these new concepts tend to yield genuinely useful math and broaden your mind about traditional notions.
cues.zh: 然后你定义新的概念，让这些模糊的发现变得说得通。而这些新概念往往会带来真正有用的数学，并拓宽你对传统观念的认识。

cues.en: So in answer to the age old question of whether math is invention or discovery, my personal belief is that discovery of nonrigorous truths is what leads us to the construction of rigorous terms that are useful, opening the door for more fuzzy discoveries continuing the cycle.
cues.zh: 所以，对于“数学是发明还是发现”这个古老问题，我的个人看法是：对非严格真理的发现，引导我们构建出有用的严格术语，从而为更多模糊发现敞开大门，让这个循环不断延续。
